practicalQuestion: What should pre-training fueling and hydration prioritize for a collegiate athlete completing an early-morning high-intensity session when appetite is low and less than 45 minutes are available before training?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athletes participating in high-intensity morning training
decisionContext.phase: Before an early-morning field or court session
decisionContext.outcome: Support session quality with a practical, tolerable intake approach
decisionContext.constraints: Low appetite; limited preparation time; individual gastrointestinal tolerance; no clinical nutrition condition

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source in the pack tests fueling or hydration in the final 45 minutes before training, low appetite, or early-morning team-sport sessions. The closest evidence is a narrative review of pre-competition carbohydrate timing set at 1 to 4 hours before exercise, a two-player glycogen case study, caffeine timing recommendations set at about 1 hour before exercise, and hydration studies from American football and elite heat competition. These sources inform options, but none directly answers the question.

dimensions.sourceReview: Two narrative reviews (rugby league nutrition; caffeine and sleep), one narrative review of elite athletes competing in heat, a two-player case study in elite Australian Football, a field study of 31 male high school football players in heat, and a validation study in 30 male American football athletes.
dimensions.directness: Low. The carbohydrate and caffeine timing guidance starts at about 1 hour or more before exercise, which is longer than the window in this question. No source addresses low appetite or very short pre-session windows.
dimensions.consistency: No material disagreement among the sources. Each source addresses a different part of the question, so there is little overlap to compare.
dimensions.transferability: Limited. The populations studied were male professional rugby league players, 2 elite male Australian Football players, male high school and post-graduate American football players, and elite athletes competing in heat. No source studied collegiate athletes, female athletes, or early-morning field or court sessions.

bottomLine.text: The library does not contain evidence on what to eat or drink in the final 45 minutes before an early-morning session when appetite is low. The available sources describe carbohydrate intake 1 to 4 hours before competition, caffeine about 1 hour before exercise, and hydration practices that are personalized and planned in advance. Use these as starting points for an individualized plan with a sports dietitian, not as a tested answer for this situation.

actions.title: Option: move the main fueling earlier
actions.text: One review suggests 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate 1 to 4 hours before competition in professional rugby league players, and its authors note that sport-specific data are limited. In a two-player case study, carbohydrate loading the day before, plus a pre-match meal, raised muscle glycogen. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): when less than 45 minutes are available, some of the carbohydrate could be moved to the previous evening's intake.

actions.title: Option: a small, practiced intake in the available window
actions.text: The evidence does not test the amount, form, or tolerance of food or fluid taken within 45 minutes of training, or how to manage low appetite. In elite athletes competing in heat, best practice included hydration strategies that were planned and practised in advance. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): trial any small pre-session intake during lower-stakes sessions before relying on it.

actions.title: Hydration: plan for the athlete and for carryover from earlier sessions
actions.text: Consensus cited in one study recommends personalized hydration practices. Some athletes become significantly dehydrated even when fluid is available. In 31 male high school football players training in heat, hydration deficits carried over between practices, mostly when there were less than 24 hours between them. A morning session after an evening session may therefore warrant a planned fluid approach.

actions.title: Option: caffeine, only if individually trialed and approved
actions.text: Two reviews describe 3 to 6 mg/kg caffeine taken about 1 hour before exercise, which is longer than the 45 minutes available here. Responses vary between individuals. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): consider caffeine only through the sports dietitian and medical staff, within institutional and governing-body rules.

monitoring.label: Hydration checks
monitoring.text: In high school football players, urine color and urine specific gravity did not significantly detect body mass changes. Do not rely on urine measures alone. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): pre- and post-session body mass may help track fluid loss across consecutive sessions.

monitoring.label: Tolerance and session quality
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): record gastrointestinal comfort, perceived energy, and session output for each pre-session intake option the athlete trials, so the plan can be adjusted to the individual.

guardrails.text: This brief informs professional judgment. It does not prescribe an individual nutrition plan. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): individual fueling and hydration plans belong with a qualified sports dietitian.

Caffeine timing evidence is set at about 1 hour before exercise, and responses vary between individuals. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): caffeine use must follow institutional and governing-body rules and should not be introduced without staff oversight.

limitations.text: No source tested intake within 45 minutes of exercise, low appetite, or early-morning team-sport training. The carbohydrate timing guidance comes from a narrative review of professional male rugby league players, and its authors note limited sport-specific data.
The glycogen evidence comes from a case study of 2 elite male Australian Football players during match play, and the authors call for larger studies.

The hydration evidence comes from male high school and post-graduate American football athletes and from elite athletes competing in heat. It may not transfer to collegiate, female, indoor court, or cooler-condition sessions.

whatCouldChange.text: Trials comparing small pre-exercise carbohydrate or fluid options taken less than 45 minutes before high-intensity team-sport training in collegiate athletes would allow a recommended direction.
Evidence on caffeine taken closer to an early-morning session, rather than about 1 hour before, in collegiate team-sport athletes.

claims.text: A narrative review of young professional male rugby league players suggests competition nutrition of 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 g/kg protein 1 to 4 hours before exercise for 80 to 120 kg players. The authors note there may not be enough data for rugby league specific recommendations.

claims.text: In a case study of 2 elite male Australian Football players, a 24-hour carbohydrate-loading protocol of 8 g/kg plus 2 g/kg in the pre-match meal raised muscle glycogen above 500 mmol/kg dry weight. The authors state this appears sufficient for elite match play.

Conclusion: Prematch CHO loading elevated muscle glycogen concentrations (ie, >500 mmol/kg dw), the magnitude of which appears sufﬁcient to meet the metabolic demands of elite AF match play.

claims.text: Two narrative reviews describe caffeine at 3 to 6 mg/kg taken about 1 hour before exercise. One describes this as the current recommendation. The other, on rugby league players, describes it as a supplement that potentially improves performance.

evidence.excerpt: The current recommendation for caffeine supplementation is ingesting ~ 3-6 mg/kg about 1 h before the onset of exercise.
Supplements that potentially improve performance, recovery, and adaptation include low to moderate dosages of caffeine (3-6 mg/kg) and ∼300 mg polyphenols consumed ∼1 hr preexercise

claims.text: A narrative review reports that the performance response to caffeine and its effect on sleep can vary between individuals and depend on session conditions such as time of onset and duration.

evidence.excerpt: Overall, the performance response to caffeine and the effect of this substance on sleep quality can vary interindividually and depend on the conditions of the exercise session (time of onset, duration, etc.).

claims.text: A narrative review of elite athletes competing in heat describes best practice as heat acclimation complemented by pre-planned and practised cooling and hydration strategies used immediately before or during competition.

evidence.excerpt: include heat acclimation/acclimatisation [(HA); i.e., long-term pre-competition preparation] complemented by pre-planned and practised cooling and hydration strategies (i.e., short-term interventions immediately before or during competition).

claims.text: In 31 male high school football players practicing outdoors in heat, urine color showed carryover effects between several practices, most of which had less than 24 hours between them.

evidence.excerpt: For Ucol, there was a carryover effect from practice numbers 2 to 3, 6 to 7 AM, 7 AM to 7 PM (p , 0.001 for all), and 10 to 11 (p 5 0.004); most with less than 24 hours between practices.

claims.text: In the same 31 male high school football players, urine color and urine specific gravity did not show significant sensitivity and specificity for detecting body mass changes.

evidence.excerpt: Sensitivity and specificity for using Ucol or USG to determine BM changes was not significant.

assumptions: Assumed the session is a typical team-sport field or court session of about 60 to 120 minutes, because duration and environmental conditions were not given.
Assumed athletes have access to a sports dietitian and that institutional and governing-body rules apply to any caffeine use.
coverageGaps: Studies of carbohydrate or food intake taken less than 45 minutes before high-intensity team-sport training
Evidence on fueling strategies for athletes with low appetite before early-morning sessions, including liquid versus solid options
Evidence on pre-session fluid volume or timing for early-morning field or court sessions
Studies in collegiate or female team-sport athletes on pre-training fueling and gastrointestinal tolerance

Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): persistent low appetite, significant weight change, or gastrointestinal symptoms should be referred to sports medicine or dietitian staff, not managed only through pre-session timing.
